title: Speech & Debate
description: Free Speech & Debate study guide: public speaking, organization, delivery, argument construction, evidence, resolution analysis, refutation and cross-examination, and the Policy, Lincoln-Douglas and Public Forum formats. 80 practice questions with explanations, 48 flashcards and a practice exam.

units.name: Public Speaking Foundations

concepts.intro: Every effective speech starts by analyzing who is listening and why.
b: Purposes: to inform, to persuade, or to entertain/commemorate (special occasion)
Audience analysis: demographics (age, background) and attitudes (knowledge, beliefs, interest)
Adapt vocabulary, examples and length to the audience and setting
A specific purpose statement names what you want the audience to know, believe or do
The occasion (classroom, ceremony, competition) shapes tone and formality

concepts.intro: Aristotle identified three modes of persuasion.
b: Ethos: credibility, from expertise, trustworthiness and goodwill
Pathos: emotional appeal through stories, vivid language and shared values
Logos: logical appeal through evidence, statistics and reasoning
Strong speeches balance all three; overreliance on pathos can seem manipulative
Kairos: the timeliness or appropriateness of an argument for the moment

concepts.intro: Nervousness is normal and manageable.
b: Most speakers feel anxious; audiences usually notice much less than the speaker feels
Preparation and repeated rehearsal out loud reduce anxiety the most
Slow breathing calms the physical stress response
Focus on the message and the audience rather than on yourself
Visualization: imagine delivering the speech successfully

keyFacts: Three general purposes: inform, persuade, entertain/commemorate.
Ethos = credibility, pathos = emotion, logos = logic.
Audience analysis: demographics and attitudes.
Rehearsing out loud is the best cure for nerves.
traps: Ethos isn't 'ethics'. It's the audience's perception of your credibility.
Informing and persuading are different goals; don't slip into advocacy in an informative speech.
Memorizing word for word often increases anxiety and sounds stiff.

units.name: Speech Organization

concepts.intro: An introduction must win attention and prepare the audience for what follows.
b: Attention-getter: a question, startling statistic, story, quotation or vivid image
Reveal the topic and relate it to the audience's lives
Establish credibility: why should they listen to you?
Thesis statement: the central idea in one sentence
Preview the main points so listeners can follow

concepts.intro: Main points should follow a clear pattern.
b: Chronological: time order (history, processes)
Spatial: physical layout (a tour of a building)
Topical: logical categories (three benefits of exercise)
Cause–effect and problem–solution patterns; Monroe's Motivated Sequence for persuasion: attention, need, satisfaction, visualization, action
Transitions and signposts ('First…', 'Now that we've seen the problem…') guide listeners

concepts.intro: End strongly and plan with outlines.
b: Signal the ending, summarize main points and restate the thesis
Close with a memorable clincher: call back to the opening, a quotation or a call to action
Don't introduce new main points in the conclusion
A preparation outline uses full sentences; a speaking outline uses brief key words
Most speeches work best with 2–5 main points

keyFacts: Intro: attention, topic, credibility, thesis, preview.
Patterns: chronological, spatial, topical, cause–effect, problem–solution.
Monroe's Motivated Sequence: attention, need, satisfaction, visualization, action.
Conclusion: summarize, restate thesis, clincher.
traps: Don't open with 'Hi, my speech is about…'. Start with an attention-getter.
New main points in the conclusion confuse listeners.
A speaking outline shouldn't be a full script.

units.name: Delivery & Body Language

concepts.intro: How a speech is delivered changes how natural it sounds.
b: Manuscript: reading word for word; precise but often monotone
Memorized: no notes, but risks forgetting and stiffness
Impromptu: little or no preparation
Extemporaneous: carefully prepared and practiced, delivered from brief notes; preferred for most speeches
Extemp competition gives speakers about 30 minutes to prepare a speech on a current-events question

concepts.intro: Your voice carries meaning beyond your words.
b: Volume: loud enough for the back row
Rate: vary speed; slow down for key ideas
Pitch and inflection: avoid monotone
Pauses create emphasis and replace filler words like 'um' and 'like'
Articulation and pronunciation make words clear and correct

concepts.intro: Body language can support or undercut your message.
b: Eye contact builds connection and credibility; scan the whole room
Gestures should be natural and purposeful, not repetitive
Posture: stand balanced and open; avoid swaying or leaning
Facial expressions should match the tone of your message
Movement can mark transitions but shouldn't be random pacing

keyFacts: Extemporaneous delivery: prepared, practiced, brief notes.
Use pauses instead of filler words.
Vary rate, pitch and volume to avoid monotone.
Eye contact builds credibility.
traps: Extemporaneous doesn't mean unprepared. That's impromptu.
Reading a manuscript word for word usually loses eye contact.
Constant hand-waving distracts; purposeful gestures help.

units.name: Argument Construction

concepts.intro: A complete argument explains why it's true and why it matters.
b: Claim: the point you're making
Warrant: the reasoning that explains why the claim is true
Evidence (data): facts, statistics, expert testimony supporting the warrant
Impact: why the claim matters (magnitude, probability, timeframe)
Toulmin model: claim, data, warrant, backing, qualifier, rebuttal

concepts.intro: Different reasoning patterns have different strengths and weaknesses.
b: Deductive reasoning moves from general principles to a specific conclusion (a syllogism)
Inductive reasoning generalizes from specific examples
Causal reasoning claims one thing causes another; watch for confounding factors
Analogical reasoning compares two similar cases
Sign reasoning infers a condition from observable signs

concepts.intro: Fallacies are errors in reasoning that can look persuasive.
b: Ad hominem: attacking the person instead of the argument
Straw man: misrepresenting an opponent's argument to attack it easily
Slippery slope: claiming one step leads inevitably to extreme consequences without evidence
False dilemma: presenting only two options when more exist
Hasty generalization, post hoc ('after this, therefore because of this'), bandwagon and appeal to authority outside expertise

keyFacts: Argument = claim + warrant + evidence + impact.
Toulmin: claim, data, warrant, backing, qualifier, rebuttal.
Deductive: general → specific; inductive: specific → general.
Ad hominem attacks the person, not the argument.
traps: Evidence isn't a warrant; you must explain how evidence proves the claim.
Correlation presented as causation is the post hoc fallacy.
Calling out a fallacy isn't enough. Explain why the reasoning fails.

units.name: Evidence & Research

concepts.intro: Strong arguments depend on reliable, relevant evidence.
b: Types: statistics, examples, expert testimony, studies, historical precedent
Use library databases, government sources, peer-reviewed journals and reputable news outlets
Search with specific keywords and operators (quotation marks, site:.gov)
Record full citation information as you research
Look for evidence on both sides so you can anticipate responses

concepts.intro: Not all sources are equally trustworthy.
b: Check the author's expertise and possible bias
Check the date: recent evidence matters for changing issues
Prefer primary sources and peer-reviewed studies over secondhand summaries
Lateral reading: check what other sources say about a site before trusting it
Be wary of evidence without a clear source, or statistics without context

concepts.intro: Using evidence honestly is both an ethical and a strategic requirement.
b: Orally cite sources: author, credentials, publication and date
Never distort a quotation's meaning by clipping out context
Explain the evidence: tell the audience what it proves
Plagiarism, presenting others' words or ideas as your own, violates ethics and competition rules
In debate, a card is a quoted piece of evidence with a full citation

keyFacts: Evaluate sources by author, bias, date and evidence quality.
Lateral reading checks a source's reputation elsewhere.
Orally cite author, credentials, publication and date.
A debate 'card' is quoted evidence with its citation.
traps: A professional-looking website isn't automatically credible.
Clipping a quotation to change its meaning is an ethics violation.
Evidence without explanation doesn't persuade judges.

units.name: Resolution Analysis

concepts.intro: A debate resolution is the statement the two sides argue about.
b: Resolutions of fact: is something true? ('Social media harms teen mental health')
Resolutions of value: which value is more important? (common in Lincoln-Douglas)
Resolutions of policy: should an actor take an action? ('The USFG should…')
The affirmative supports the resolution; the negative opposes it
Presumption often favors the status quo, so the affirmative carries the burden of proof

concepts.intro: Definitions frame the whole debate.
b: Identify every key term in the resolution and find credible definitions
Topicality: whether the affirmative's case actually falls within the resolution
Look at the actor, the action and the object (who does what to what)
Consider ground: definitions should leave fair arguments for both sides
Framework: the lens (value, criterion or weighing mechanism) judges should use

concepts.intro: Policy affirmatives traditionally must prove several stock issues.
b: Harms: a significant problem exists
Inherency: the status quo won't solve it on its own
Solvency: the plan would solve the problem
Topicality: the plan fits the resolution
Significance and advantages: the benefits outweigh disadvantages

keyFacts: Resolution types: fact, value, policy.
Affirmative supports; negative opposes.
Stock issues: harms, inherency, solvency, topicality, significance.
Topicality asks whether the case fits the resolution.
traps: Value resolutions aren't settled by facts alone; they need a weighing framework.
Inherency isn't the harm itself. It's why the status quo won't fix the harm.
Definitions that leave the other side no ground are often rejected by judges.

units.name: Refutation & Crossfire

concepts.intro: Refutation directly answers an opponent's argument.
b: Step 1, 'They say': summarize the opponent's argument fairly
Step 2, 'But': state your response
Step 3, 'Because': give reasoning and evidence
Step 4, 'Therefore': explain the impact on the round
Signpost which argument you're answering so the judge can follow on the flow

concepts.intro: Different attacks weaken arguments in different ways.
b: Deny: the evidence or reasoning is false
Minimize: the impact is smaller than claimed
Turn: the argument actually supports your side (a link or impact turn)
Outweigh: even if true, your impacts are bigger, more likely or sooner
Point out dropped arguments: an argument not answered is usually treated as conceded

concepts.intro: Questioning periods clarify arguments and expose weaknesses.
b: Ask short, focused questions with a clear goal
Use questions to set up arguments you'll make in your next speech
Don't make speeches during questioning or ask open-ended questions that let opponents repeat their case
When answering, stay calm, be concise and don't concede more than necessary
Public Forum 'crossfire' lets both speakers question each other; 'grand crossfire' involves all four

keyFacts: Refutation: They say → But → Because → Therefore.
Responses: deny, minimize, turn, outweigh.
Dropped arguments are usually treated as conceded.
Flowing: taking organized notes on every argument.
traps: Misrepresenting the opponent's argument before refuting it is a straw man.
Cross-ex isn't a time for speeches.
Answering some arguments well can still lose if you drop a key one.

units.name: Event Formats (CX, LD, PF)

concepts.intro: Two-person teams debate whether the government should adopt a specific plan.
b: Teams of two; a year-long policy resolution
Structure: four constructive speeches, each followed by cross-examination, then four rebuttals
Evidence-heavy; debaters often speak very quickly
Affirmative presents a plan; negative may run disadvantages, counterplans, topicality and kritiks
Named 'CX' for its cross-examination periods

concepts.intro: One-on-one debate focused on values and philosophy.
b: Named for the 1858 Lincoln–Douglas Senate debates
Resolutions usually ask a value question and change every two months
Each side presents a value (e.g. justice) and a criterion that measures it (e.g. protecting rights)
Speeches: AC, cross-ex, NC, cross-ex, 1AR, NR, 2AR
Philosophers such as Kant, Mill, Locke and Rawls often appear

concepts.intro: Two-person teams debate current events for a general audience.
b: Created to be accessible to lay judges and audiences
Resolutions change monthly and address current events
A coin toss decides side and speaking order
Speeches: constructive, rebuttal, summary and final focus, with crossfire periods including grand crossfire
Emphasizes clear communication and evidence-based argument without a formal plan

keyFacts: CX: two-person teams, policy plan, evidence-heavy.
LD: one-on-one, value and criterion.
PF: two-person teams, current events, lay judges, coin toss.
LD is named after the 1858 Lincoln–Douglas debates.
traps: LD is one-on-one; CX and PF are two-person teams.
PF teams don't present formal plans the way CX affirmatives do.
A criterion isn't a second value. It's how you measure the value.

quiz.q: A speech explaining how vaccines train the immune system has the general purpose to:
quiz.e: It explains rather than advocates.

quiz.q: Citing your five years as a certified EMT before discussing CPR builds:
quiz.e: Relevant expertise increases credibility.

quiz.q: Telling the story of a single family affected by a flood primarily uses:
quiz.e: Personal stories evoke emotion.

quiz.q: Presenting statistics on crash rates before and after a seat-belt law uses:
quiz.e: Evidence and reasoning appeal to logic.

quiz.q: Audience analysis includes examining:
o: The speaker's preferred seating layout, volume and lighting
The speaker's own vocabulary, humor and personal habits
The audience's knowledge, attitudes and demographics
The time of day, the room temperature and the event budget
quiz.e: Knowing listeners lets you adapt your message.

quiz.q: A specific purpose statement should:
o: Name the speech's main topic in a catchy, memorable phrase
List the organizational pattern and every main point in order
Pose a question that the audience should answer during the speech
State exactly what you want the audience to know, believe or do
quiz.e: E.g. 'To persuade my audience to register to vote.'

quiz.q: The most effective way to reduce speaking anxiety is:
quiz.e: Familiarity with the material builds confidence.

quiz.q: Kairos refers to:
quiz.e: Arguments are more persuasive when they fit the moment.

quiz.q: A eulogy is an example of which type of speech?
quiz.e: It honors a person at a ceremony.

quiz.q: Why might relying mostly on pathos backfire?
o: Audiences may feel manipulated if emotion isn't backed by evidence
Audiences may find the speaker too logical and less credible overall
Emotional appeals are rejected by judges in every debate format
Heavy emotion makes the speech too long to deliver in time
quiz.e: Balance emotion with logic and credibility.

quiz.q: Which is the strongest attention-getter?
o: 'Many people have strong opinions about how safe our homes really are.'
'Before I begin, let me thank you all for having me today.'
'Every 11 seconds, someone in the U.S. visits an emergency room after a fall.'
'According to the dictionary, a fall is defined as an accident.'
quiz.e: A striking fact grabs attention.

quiz.q: A speech on the history of the internet from 1969 to today would likely use which pattern?
quiz.e: Time order suits history.

quiz.q: A tour of the parts of a volcano from base to crater uses:
quiz.e: Organized by physical location.

quiz.q: Monroe's Motivated Sequence ends with:
quiz.e: Attention, need, satisfaction, visualization, action.

quiz.q: The preview in an introduction:
o: Lists the main points to come
quiz.e: It prepares listeners to follow the structure.

quiz.q: Phrases like 'My second point is…' are:
quiz.e: They mark where you are in the speech.

quiz.q: A persuasive speech that describes a school lunch problem and then proposes a fix uses:
quiz.e: Problem then solution.

quiz.q: What should a conclusion NOT do?
quiz.e: New points belong in the body.

quiz.q: A speaking outline differs from a preparation outline because it:
o: Uses brief key words and delivery cues
quiz.e: It's a brief memory aid.

quiz.q: How many main points do most short speeches have?
quiz.e: Too many points overwhelm listeners.

quiz.q: Which delivery method is carefully practiced but delivered from brief notes?
quiz.e: It balances preparation with natural delivery.

quiz.q: Speaking with almost no preparation is:
quiz.e: Impromptu speeches are given on the spot.

quiz.q: A good replacement for filler words like 'um' is:
quiz.e: Pauses sound confident and add emphasis.

quiz.q: Speaking in the same pitch throughout is called:
quiz.e: Varying pitch keeps listeners engaged.

quiz.q: Why is eye contact important?
o: It lets you read the audience's notes
quiz.e: Audiences trust speakers who look at them.

quiz.q: Clear, crisp pronunciation of each sound is:
quiz.e: Articulation is how clearly you form sounds.

quiz.q: Which gesture habit is most distracting?
o: Holding still during a key pause
quiz.e: Repetitive gestures pull attention away.

quiz.q: Slowing your rate is most useful when:
o: Telling an exciting, fast-paced story to build momentum
Moving through a transition or a minor background detail
Delivering a key idea or complex information
Reading the roadmap while the time signal is approaching
quiz.e: Slowing gives listeners time to absorb it.

quiz.q: A manuscript delivery is most appropriate when:
o: Delivering an informal toast at a family celebration
Responding to an audience question in an open discussion
Exact wording is essential, such as an official statement
Sharing a funny personal anecdote with a small group
quiz.e: Precision matters more than spontaneity.

quiz.q: Pacing back and forth without purpose tends to:
quiz.e: Movement should mark transitions.

quiz.q: In an argument, the warrant is:
o: The central statement the speaker wants the audience to accept
A specific statistic or quotation offered as proof
The reasoning connecting evidence to the claim
A response that attacks the opposing side's reasoning
quiz.e: It explains why the claim follows.

quiz.q: 'My opponent's plan is wrong because he's never had a real job' is:
quiz.e: It attacks the person rather than the argument.

quiz.q: 'If we allow phones at lunch, soon students will use them in every class and grades will collapse' is:
quiz.e: It predicts an extreme chain without evidence.

quiz.q: 'Either we ban all cars or accept pollution forever' is:
quiz.e: It ignores other options.

quiz.q: 'My opponent wants to cut school funding to zero' when they proposed a 5% cut is a:
quiz.e: It misrepresents the position to make it easier to attack.

quiz.q: Reasoning from several specific cases to a general conclusion is:
quiz.e: Induction generalizes from examples.

quiz.q: 'All mammals breathe air; whales are mammals; therefore whales breathe air' is:
quiz.e: It moves from a general premise to a specific conclusion.

quiz.q: The impact of an argument explains:
quiz.e: Impacts are weighed by magnitude, probability and timeframe.

quiz.q: 'I wore my lucky socks and we won, so the socks caused the win' is:
quiz.e: Sequence alone doesn't prove causation.

quiz.q: In the Toulmin model, a qualifier:
o: Answers an opponent's objection by attacking their evidence
Limits the strength of the claim (e.g. 'usually')
Supplies the main data or testimony that supports the claim
Gives the background assumption that links evidence to claim
quiz.e: Qualifiers show how certain the claim is.

quiz.q: Which source is generally most credible for a claim about medical treatment?
o: A well-written article from a popular lifestyle magazine
A testimonial from a celebrity who tried the treatment
A press release from a company that sells the treatment
quiz.e: Peer review and expert authorship add reliability.

quiz.q: Lateral reading means:
o: Checking what other sources say about a website
Reading a long page sideways by scanning across each paragraph
Reading only the abstract and conclusion of a long article
Skimming a page quickly to find the key words and dates
quiz.e: Fact-checkers leave the site to verify it.

quiz.q: An oral citation in a speech should include:
o: The author, their credentials, the publication and the date
Only the web address and the date you accessed the page
The title of the article and the page number alone
Nothing, since the written bibliography handles all citations
quiz.e: Listeners need enough to judge credibility.

quiz.q: Why does the date of evidence matter?
o: Situations and data change over time
quiz.e: Outdated evidence can mislead.

quiz.q: In debate, a 'card' is:
o: A vocabulary flashcard used to memorize key debate terms
A quoted piece of evidence with its full citation
The ballot on which a judge records the round's decision
A signal held up by the timekeeper to show time left
quiz.e: Debaters read cards as evidence.

quiz.q: Removing words from a quotation so it says the opposite of the author's meaning is:
quiz.e: It misrepresents the source.

quiz.q: A statistic with no source or context should be:
quiz.e: Unverifiable numbers can't support claims.

quiz.q: Researching evidence for the opposing side helps you:
quiz.e: Preparation for refutation.

quiz.q: Using a search operator like site:.gov helps you:
o: Search only for images and videos posted by news outlets
Remove all government sources from the search results
Automatically translate the pages into your own language
quiz.e: Operators narrow searches.

quiz.q: After reading evidence in a speech, you should:
o: Move straight on to the next point and trust it speaks for itself
Explain what it proves and how it supports your claim
Read a second card on the same point with no commentary
Apologize if the evidence was longer than you had planned
quiz.e: Evidence needs a warrant.

quiz.q: 'The United States federal government should substantially increase investment in renewable energy' is a resolution of:
quiz.e: It calls for an actor to take an action.

quiz.q: 'Justice ought to be valued above security' is a resolution of:
quiz.e: It asks which value is more important.

quiz.q: The side that supports the resolution is the:
quiz.e: The negative opposes it.

quiz.q: In policy debate, inherency is:
o: Why the status quo won't solve the problem
How large and serious the harm is for those affected
Whether the proposed plan would actually solve the problem
Whether the plan falls within the topic of the resolution
quiz.e: It shows the problem persists without the plan.

quiz.q: Solvency asks:
o: Would the plan solve the problem?
quiz.e: The affirmative must show the plan works.

quiz.q: A negative argument that the affirmative plan doesn't fit the resolution is:
quiz.e: It says the case is outside the topic.

quiz.q: Presumption in debate usually favors:
quiz.e: The affirmative bears the burden of proving change is needed.

quiz.q: Why must debaters define key terms?
o: Judges require debaters to read dictionary entries aloud
Reading definitions helps fill the allotted speaking time
Definitions set the scope of what can be argued
A definition automatically wins the argument for its side
quiz.e: They frame both sides' ground.

quiz.q: Harms in a policy case refer to:
o: The expense of carrying out the affirmative's proposal
A significant problem in the status quo
The negative's response to the affirmative's case
The judge's reasons for deciding the round
quiz.e: Harms establish why action is needed.

quiz.q: 'Ground' in resolution analysis means:
o: The physical space where a debate round takes place
The arguments fairly available to each side
The judge's personal preferences about how to weigh arguments
The closing speech that summarizes the round's issues
quiz.e: Fair definitions preserve ground for both sides.

quiz.q: The first step of four-step refutation is to:
quiz.e: 'They say…' shows the judge what you're answering.

quiz.q: Arguing that your opponent's evidence actually proves your side is a:
quiz.e: A turn flips the argument's direction.

quiz.q: 'Even if their impact happens, ours affects millions more people' is:
quiz.e: It compares impacts rather than denying them.

quiz.q: An argument the other side never answers is usually:
quiz.e: Dropped arguments generally stand.

quiz.q: 'Flowing' in debate means:
o: Speaking smoothly and without pauses from start to finish
Taking organized notes on each argument through the round
Reading evidence cards aloud at a very fast pace
Switching between the affirmative and negative sides
quiz.e: The flow tracks what's been said and answered.

quiz.q: A good cross-examination question is:
o: An open-ended question inviting them to restate their entire case
A long statement that lays out your own arguments first
A sharp personal remark that questions their intelligence
Short, focused and aimed at a specific weakness
quiz.e: Control the exchange with targeted questions.

quiz.q: In Public Forum, 'grand crossfire' involves:
quiz.e: Both teams question each other together.

quiz.q: Arguing that the harm is real but much smaller than claimed is:
quiz.e: It reduces the impact's weight.

quiz.q: When answering cross-ex questions, you should:
o: Respond with lengthy speeches that restate your whole case
Decline to answer any question that seems difficult
Stay concise and avoid conceding more than needed
Accept every assumption built into the questioner's wording
quiz.e: Composure and precision protect your case.

quiz.q: Signposting during refutation helps because:
o: It stretches the speech so that it fills all the time
The judge can match your answers to the arguments on the flow
It substitutes for the need to present supporting evidence
It confuses the opposing team about which points you made
quiz.e: Clarity wins rounds.

quiz.q: Which debate format is one-on-one and focused on values?
quiz.e: LD pits one debater against another on a value resolution.

quiz.q: Lincoln-Douglas debate is named after:
quiz.e: Abraham Lincoln and Stephen Douglas debated in 1858.

quiz.q: In LD, the criterion is:
o: A second value that the debater must also defend
The standard used to measure whether the value is achieved
The opponent's strongest argument against the resolution
The closing speech that summarizes the round
quiz.e: E.g. value: justice; criterion: protecting individual rights.

quiz.q: Which format uses a coin toss to decide sides and is designed for lay judges?
quiz.e: PF aims to be accessible to general audiences.

quiz.q: Policy debate is often called 'CX' because of its:
quiz.e: Each constructive is followed by cross-ex.

quiz.q: In policy debate, the affirmative usually presents:
quiz.e: The plan is a specific policy action.

quiz.q: A negative argument that the plan causes a harmful side effect is a:
quiz.e: Disadvantages weigh against the plan's advantages.

quiz.q: Public Forum resolutions typically change:
quiz.e: They track current events.

quiz.q: The last speech in a Public Forum round is the:
quiz.e: It crystallizes why the team should win.

quiz.q: Which philosopher's ideas might an LD debater use to argue that outcomes (the greatest good) matter most?
quiz.e: Mill's utilitarianism weighs consequences.

quiz.q: A speech whose general purpose is to persuade aims to:
o: Teach the audience a skill without taking any position
Entertain the audience with humor or a memorable story
Present facts about a topic in a neutral, balanced way
Change or reinforce beliefs or actions
quiz.e: Informative speeches teach; persuasive speeches move the audience.

quiz.q: Audience analysis helps a speaker:
o: Tailor content to listeners' needs and views
Reduce eye contact and rely on the manuscript
Cut the speech down to fit a shorter time limit
Memorize the script word for word before delivery
quiz.e: Know who you are speaking to before choosing examples.

quiz.q: Ethos is an appeal based on:
quiz.e: Logos is logic; pathos is emotion.

quiz.q: Which is the best way to manage nervousness?
quiz.e: Familiarity reduces anxiety.

quiz.q: A strong introduction usually:
o: States the final conclusion before any evidence is given
Begins with an apology for being nervous and unprepared
Reads the complete list of sources used in the speech
Gets attention and previews the main points
quiz.e: The introduction gains attention and states the thesis.

quiz.q: A transition helps a speech by:
quiz.e: Signposts guide the audience.

quiz.q: A speech that arranges points by time order is:
quiz.e: Chronological order follows a sequence of events.

quiz.q: A conclusion should:
o: Apologize for any mistakes made during the speech
Introduce several new main points the audience has not heard
Summarize and leave a final impression
Repeat the introduction word for word with no changes
quiz.e: End with a memorable closing thought.

quiz.q: Problem-solution organization is best for:
o: Explaining a process step by step
Persuading people to adopt a fix
quiz.e: It shows an issue, then a response.

quiz.q: Good eye contact means:
o: Looking at different people throughout the audience
Staring at one friendly person for the whole speech
Looking down at the floor or at the back wall
Reading the speech entirely from the page or screen
quiz.e: Scanning the room builds connection.

quiz.q: Vocal variety includes changes in:
quiz.e: Variety keeps listeners engaged.

quiz.q: Filler words such as 'um' can be reduced by:
quiz.e: A pause is better than a filler.

quiz.q: Effective gestures are usually:
quiz.e: Gestures should support the message.

quiz.q: In argumentation, a claim is:
o: A direct quotation taken from an expert source
A question that the audience is asked to answer
A published source that the speaker cites as proof
A statement you want the audience to accept
quiz.e: Claims need support.

quiz.q: A warrant explains:
quiz.e: Claim, evidence and warrant make an argument.

quiz.q: The Toulmin model includes:
quiz.e: Stephen Toulmin's model breaks down arguments into parts.

quiz.q: An argument that relies on a vague generalization from too few cases is a:
quiz.e: Small samples cannot prove broad claims.

quiz.q: The 'ad hominem' fallacy attacks:
o: The person instead of the argument
quiz.e: It avoids the real issue.

quiz.q: The most credible type of source is usually:
o: An anonymous post that has been shared widely online
A meme that has no listed source or author
A recent peer-reviewed or reputable primary source

PART_B1.q: An audience of retirees versus an audience of middle schoolers should change a speaker's:
A speech's conclusion restates the thesis and ends with a callback to the opening story. The callback is the:
'Crime rose after the new mayor took office, so the mayor caused it' commits:
A source's website looks professional, but other outlets report it's funded by the industry it reviews. This check is:

PART_B1.e: The case falls outside the resolution.

o: 'Can you explain your whole case again?'
'Your evidence is from 2009. Has the policy changed since then?'
PART_B1.e: Specific and targeted at a weakness.

PART_B1.q: In Public Forum, why do teams avoid highly technical jargon?
o: Judges are often lay community members
PART_B1.e: PF is designed for general audiences.

PART_B2.q: Build a complete argument (claim, warrant, evidence, impact) for or against a four-day school week.
PART_B2.sa: A strong answer has all four parts. Claim: 'A four-day week improves student attendance.' Warrant: fewer days reduce burnout and let appointments happen on the off day. Evidence: a credible cited study or district report on attendance changes. Impact: higher attendance means more instructional time and better outcomes, weighed by magnitude or probability. It uses a qualifier where evidence is limited.

PART_B2.q: Your opponent argues that raising the minimum wage will cause job losses. Refute it using the four-step method.
PART_B2.sa: They say: raising the minimum wage causes job losses. But: the effects are small or mixed. Because: cite credible research finding small employment effects from moderate increases, or explain higher consumer spending and lower turnover. Therefore: the impact is minimized and outweighed by higher incomes for millions of workers. Strong answers signpost clearly and weigh impacts.

PART_C.q: Write an outline for a 5-minute persuasive speech on a school issue using Monroe's Motivated Sequence. Include an attention-getter, thesis and clincher, and identify where you use ethos, pathos and logos.
PART_C.sa: A strong outline labels all five steps: attention (a striking statistic or story, identified as pathos or logos), need (problem with evidence, logos), satisfaction (a specific, feasible solution), visualization (a vivid picture of the future with and without the solution, pathos), and action (a clear, specific request). It includes a one-sentence thesis, a credibility statement (ethos) in the introduction, transitions between steps, and a clincher that calls back to the opening.

PART_C.q: Compare Lincoln-Douglas and Public Forum debate: structure, type of resolution, and what judges look for. Which better prepares students for civic life? Defend your answer.
PART_C.sa: LD is one-on-one, uses value resolutions with a value and criterion, and rewards philosophical reasoning and clash. PF uses two-person teams, monthly current-events topics and crossfire, and was designed for lay judges, rewarding clear, evidence-based communication. A strong essay then takes a defended position, e.g. PF for accessible, evidence-based discussion of current policy, or LD for ethical reasoning, supported with specific features of each format.

workedExamples.title: Claim, evidence, warrant
workedExamples.prompt: Build a short argument for 'Schools should start later.'
steps: Claim: schools should start later
Evidence: studies show teens sleep better and perform better with later starts
Warrant: better sleep leads to better learning, which is a goal of school
workedExamples.answer: Claim: start later; evidence: sleep and performance studies; warrant: learning improves with sleep

workedExamples.title: Refutation structure

steps: Say what they argued

workedExamples.answer: Adapt vocabulary, examples and length to the audience.

workedExamples.title: Outlining a speech
workedExamples.prompt: Outline a three-point speech on why students should volunteer.
steps: Introduction: attention getter, thesis and preview.

workedExamples.answer: A clear structure helps listeners follow your argument.

workedExamples.title: Reducing filler words
workedExamples.prompt: How can you cut down on saying 'um'?
steps: Record yourself to notice how often you say it.

Practice out loud until the pauses feel natural.
workedExamples.answer: Pauses sound confident and let listeners absorb your points.

workedExamples.title: Citing evidence aloud
workedExamples.prompt: How do you cite a statistic during a speech?
steps: Name the source so listeners can judge credibility.
Give the date so they know it is current.
Then state the fact clearly.

workedExamples.title: Defining a resolution
workedExamples.prompt: Break down the resolution: 'This house believes homework should be abolished.'
steps: Define the key terms, such as homework and abolished.
Identify the status quo: homework is assigned in most schools.
Decide the burden of proof: the affirmative must show abolishing homework is better.
workedExamples.answer: The affirmative argues that abolition improves learning more than it harms.

workedExamples.title: Choosing a debate format

steps: Lincoln-Douglas is one-on-one and values-focused.
